passage: Two hours before the ward meeting, rain flooded the lane and the printer at the corner shop died. Jagdish and Sarita had forty leaflets to finish by hand, about the builder's plan to fence the old maidan. Sarita pushed her phone at him. "Look, a forward says the builder bribed the corporator. Put it on the leaflet. People will be furious." Jagdish read it twice. No source, no name. "If it's false, we lose everyone who trusts us," he said, and left it off. At the meeting the builder's manager, Mr Salve, spoke first, nervous, reading from a sheet. A man behind Jagdish shouted, "Thief!" Jagdish turned round. "He's doing his job. Let him finish." When his own turn came, he stuck to the map, the children's cricket matches, the rainwater that drains into the ground. Mr Salve nodded at a few points. Sarita, wet and cross, admitted afterwards, "They listened more than I expected."

qa.q: How many leaflets did Jagdish and Sarita have to finish by hand?
qa.a: They had forty leaflets to finish by hand.

qa.q: What was Jagdish worried about when he read the forward twice?
qa.a: He was worried that an unproven claim might be false and cost them the trust of everyone who believed in the campaign.

qa.q: Which of Jagdish's choices kept the campaign credible?
qa.a: He left out the unsourced claim, defended Mr Salve's right to speak, and stuck to facts like the map, the cricket matches and the drainage.

qa.q: How did Sarita see things by the end?
qa.a: She was wet and cross but admitted people listened more than she expected, so the careful approach surprised her.

grounding: Shows a volunteer staying firm on his cause while checking facts and treating the opponent's representative as a person.

passage: By Thursday Binita had slept four hours a night for a week. The flood-relief collection drive at the community hall ended on Sunday; her office report was due Friday; her mother had left three voice notes she hadn't played. At 11 p.m. she was still sorting donated blankets, eyes stinging, when her manager emailed: "Second missed deadline this month. Let's talk." Her stomach dropped. Kishore, who ran the drive with her, found her sitting on a pile of blankets. "Go home," he said. "I can't. If I leave, the Friday van won't get loaded." "Then let Rukmini and Faisal load it. They've asked twice." A hot wave of guilt went through her. Handing it over felt like quitting. Kishore sat down beside her. "You're not the drive. You're one of eleven. Let us carry it tomorrow." Slowly she wrote the list for Rukmini, then called her mother back on the walk home.

qa.q: How many voice notes had Binita's mother left?
qa.a: Her mother had left three voice notes.

qa.q: Why did handing over the Friday van feel so hard for Binita?
qa.a: She felt guilty, as if slowing down meant quitting on the people the drive was serving.

qa.q: What did Kishore suggest that could help the work last?
qa.a: Share the load: let Rukmini and Faisal load the van, since she is one of eleven, not the whole drive.

qa.q: How might Rukmini and Faisal feel about finally being handed the task?
qa.a: Having asked twice, they probably feel relieved and trusted to carry part of the work.

grounding: Shows a committed volunteer whose work, sleep and family suffer, who feels guilty slowing down, and who learns to share the load.

passage:
Week one. At the first meeting of the campaign to save the night bus, Amandeep noticed only Harpal, who spoke standing on a chair and got every cheer. Dilnaz sat in a corner, writing names in a notebook. Amandeep privately thought she wasn't doing much.
Week three. The petition had 2,000 signatures. Amandeep asked who had organised the door-to-door rounds. It was Dilnaz, with a spreadsheet of every lane and every volunteer's free hours. Old Mr Fernandes, who couldn't walk far, had paid for the printing. A college student, Moumita, had written the letter to the transport office.
Week five. At the hearing, Harpal spoke brilliantly. When the room clapped, he pulled Dilnaz up to stand beside him. Amandeep clapped hardest for her, and felt a little ashamed of week one.

qa.q: How many signatures did the petition have in week three?
qa.a: The petition had 2,000 signatures.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep feel a little ashamed in week five?
qa.a: Amandeep had privately dismissed Dilnaz in week one, and now saw how much her quiet organising had achieved.

qa.q: What could a campaign do to reduce resentment between members?
qa.a: Name and thank the quieter roles, like Dilnaz's spreadsheet, Mr Fernandes's printing and Moumita's letter, as Harpal did by pulling Dilnaz up.

qa.q: What might it feel like for Dilnaz when Harpal pulls her up to stand beside him?
qa.a: She may feel surprised and seen, after weeks of work that few people noticed.

grounding: Amandeep, watching over five weeks, sees that the campaign needs organisers, funders and writers, not only its loudest speaker.

passage: On the third day of the Silchar floods, the relief camp in the school building had no power after dark. Neelam had been handing out dry rations since six in the morning, her feet soaked through her sandals. Irfan, the volunteer coordinator, had one rule: nobody goes into the water on their own. At dusk a man ran in shouting that his neighbour's family was stuck on a roof two lanes away. Neelam's whole body wanted to run. She grabbed her torch. Irfan caught her arm. "Neelam. Write it down. Lane, house, how many people. The boat team goes, not you." She wrote it with shaking hands, and he radioed it through. Twenty minutes later the boat's lamp swung across the dark water. Neelam went back to the ration line, handed a packet to a crying girl, and suddenly had to sit down on the steps. Irfan brought her tea and said nothing.

qa.q: What was Irfan's one rule?
qa.a: Nobody goes into the water on their own.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when she suddenly sat down on the steps?
qa.a: She was exhausted and overwhelmed after the long day and the fear for the family on the roof.

qa.q: Why was writing down the details wiser than running to the roof?
qa.a: It got the trained boat team there quickly while keeping Neelam safe, so the help stayed effective instead of adding another person to rescue.

qa.q: How might Irfan have felt when he caught Neelam's arm?
qa.a: He was probably worried for her safety and firm about it, knowing the organised boat team could do more than one brave volunteer alone.

grounding: Shows a young flood-relief volunteer, tired, useful and overwhelmed, whose help stays safe and effective inside an organised effort.

subtype: Staying safe and lawful in action [Response]
passage: Gopika, people think organising a march is all slogans. For me, Vishal, it's mostly lists. Before our farmers' solidarity walk in Nashik, we got police permission in writing, printed copies and gave one to every marshal. We had twelve marshals in orange bibs, a first-aid volunteer, water every half kilometre, and one rule printed on every card: if anything turns violent, we walk away. Halfway, near the market, a group none of us knew joined at the back and started throwing stones at a shop shutter. Some of our young ones wanted to stay and argue. I blew the whistle, the marshals turned the front of the march into the side road, and we finished at the temple ground as planned. Later a reporter asked if we ran away. I said yes. A good cause doesn't need a broken shutter.

qa.q: How many marshals were there?
qa.a: Twelve marshals in orange bibs.

qa.q: How did Vishal feel when the reporter asked if they ran away?
qa.a: Vishal felt calm and sure, even proud, saying yes because a good cause needs no broken shutter.

qa.q: Which safety steps made the march work?
qa.a: Written police permission, marshals with copies, first aid, water, and a clear rule to walk away if violence starts, which Vishal followed.

qa.q: How might the young marchers who wanted to stay and argue have felt?
qa.a: They may have felt frustrated or even embarrassed to leave, but were safer, since staying could have tied them to the violence.

grounding: Vishal describes planning a march for safety and legality and leading it away when others turned violent.

subtype: Pressure to protect the institution's name [Receiver]
passage: Placement week, and Saurabh was called to the HOD's cabin between two interviews. Dr Hemant Joshi didn't offer him a seat. "You emailed the university about the leaked mid-sem paper?" "Sir, I saw it shared in the hostel group the night before." "And did you think of the college's name? Of the companies sitting downstairs right now? Of your batchmates' jobs?" Two other professors in the room said nothing, eyes on their files. Dr Joshi slid a sheet across. "A simple withdrawal. You were mistaken. Everyone moves on." Saurabh's mouth went dry. He felt, absurdly, like the one who had cheated. His next interview was in ten minutes. He picked up the pen. Then he put it down. "Sir, can I think about it tonight?" In the corridor he called his aunt, a lecturer in Pune. "Don't sign anything under pressure," she said. "Tonight we'll read the university's grievance rules together."

qa.q: What had Saurabh emailed the university about?
qa.a: About the leaked mid-sem paper.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling as Dr Joshi slid the withdrawal sheet across?
qa.a: He felt afraid and strangely guilty, as if he were the one who had cheated, with a dry mouth and an interview ten minutes away.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do that protected him, and what else could help?
qa.a: He didn't sign under pressure and asked for time, then called his aunt; reading the grievance rules with her is a safe next step.

qa.q: What might the two silent professors have been thinking?
qa.a: They may have felt uneasy about the pressure but afraid to cross the HOD, so they kept their eyes on their files.

grounding: Shows a student who reported cheating being told it will harm the college's name, feeling guilt and fear, and nearly withdrawing.

passage:
"Is this seat free?" Hemant asked. The three at the table glanced at one another. "Saving it," said Rishabh, not looking up.
Hemant moved to the corner. Two tables away someone muttered, "That's the one who got Nikhil sir suspended."
"Nikhil sir was taking money for marks," Hemant said, to nobody.
Leela set her tray down opposite him. "Mind if I sit?"
"You sure? They'll talk about you too."
"Let them. Did you eat anything today?"
"No. Nobody's said a word to me since Monday. Not rude. Just nothing. They stop talking when I walk in."
"I know. I've watched it." She pushed half her samosa across. "For what it's worth, you did the right thing. My brother paid him last year. He still feels sick about it."
Hemant laughed, shakily. "One person. That's all it takes, huh?"
"Also, the grievance committee handles retaliation. I'll come with you to the dean tomorrow if you want."
"Yeah. Okay."

qa.q: What was Nikhil sir doing, according to Hemant?
qa.a: Nikhil sir was taking money for marks.

qa.q: How was Hemant feeling as he sat alone in the corner?
qa.a: He felt isolated and hurt, since nobody had spoken to him since Monday, though he still believed the report was right.

qa.q: How did Leela support Hemant in practical ways?
qa.a: She sat with him, shared food, told him he did the right thing, and offered to go with him to the dean tomorrow.

qa.q: Why might Rishabh and the others be avoiding Hemant?
qa.a: They may fear being linked to him, or feel loyal to the teacher, so quiet avoidance feels safer than taking a side.

grounding: Shows a student isolated and gossiped about after reporting wrongdoing, and how much one ally's support matters.

subtype: Told to stay quiet at work [Receiver]
passage: You asked about the hardest week on site. That's easy. I'm Mohit, junior site engineer, and in March I found cracks in the base plates of the scaffolding on Tower B. Forty workers climbed it every morning. I showed Tanvir sir, my manager. He looked at the photos and said, "Mohit, the client visit is Friday. It's held for two years. Don't make noise, for the company's sake." For a whole night I doubted my own eyes. Maybe I'm new. Maybe I'm wrong. Maybe I lose the job. But at six in the morning I taped off Tower B myself and wrote it in the site safety register with the photos and the time. Then I went to the safety officer, who came up with me, looked, and stopped all work on that tower. Tanvir sir didn't speak to me for two weeks. The scaffold was replaced by Wednesday.

qa.q: Where did Mohit find the cracks?
qa.a: In the base plates of the scaffolding on Tower B.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling during that long night?
qa.a: Mohit felt afraid of losing the job and full of doubt, wondering whether being new meant being wrong.

qa.q: Which steps did Mohit take that protected the workers and the truth?
qa.a: Taping off Tower B, recording the problem with photos and time in the safety register, and taking it to the safety officer, who stopped work.

qa.q: How might the forty workers see Mohit's choice if they knew?
qa.a: They would likely feel grateful and safer, since their lives were on that scaffolding every morning.

grounding: Mohit describes being told by a manager to let a safety problem go, feeling fear and self-doubt, and acting to protect the workers anyway.

passage:
Supervisor's note, quality lab, Friday.
Today Pema, 25, came to my desk and asked to speak privately. For four months, she said, the cold-room temperature logs had been "tidied". It began in February, when the logger failed one night and Noor, the senior technician, filled in the missing readings from memory. "Everyone does it," Noor told her. "It protects the team." The next week Pema copied one reading. Then a whole night. By May she was writing numbers without looking at the gauge. She said the guilt got quieter each time, and that frightened her more than the guilt. She was pale and kept apologising. I thanked her for coming and said I would deal with the logs and the process, not her character. Next: this afternoon I pulled the affected batches for testing, informed the plant head in writing, and asked for a meeting with Noor and HR on Monday.

qa.q: When did the tidying of the temperature logs begin?
qa.a: It began in February, when the logger failed one night.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling as the guilt grew quieter?
qa.a: Pema was frightened that the guilt got quieter each time, even more than by the guilt itself.

qa.q: What did the supervisor do next, and why does it matter?
qa.a: The supervisor pulled the affected batches for testing, informed the plant head in writing and set a meeting, which protects people and fixes the process.

qa.q: How might Noor see the tidying that started it all?
qa.a: Noor seems to see it as harmless team protection, saying "everyone does it", without facing how each step made the next easier.

grounding: The supervisor's note shows Pema sliding step by step into a cover-up, each fudged reading easier than the last, until she speaks up.

passage:
Mahima,
I need to write this to someone outside the office.
You know Sethi ma'am took me on when no one else would, after I failed my exams twice. The team is like family; we eat from one another's tiffins. Last month I found that the grant for the girls' hostel roof has been moved, quietly, into salaries. On paper the roof is "in progress". In real life, the girls in the top dorm put buckets under the leaks every night.
When I asked, ma'am said, "Vikas, trust me. We'll fix it next quarter." Ravi from accounts told me not to be "the traitor who breaks us".
Both things feel true. I love these people. And thirty girls are sleeping under a leaking roof.
I keep drafting an email to the board and deleting it. I'm scared.
Tell me I'm not crazy.
Vikas

qa.q: What was the grant meant for?
qa.a: The grant was meant for the girls' hostel roof.

qa.q: What is Vikas feeling while drafting and deleting the email?
qa.a: Vikas feels torn and scared: grateful and loyal to Sethi ma'am and the team, but troubled by the girls under the leaking roof.

qa.q: What would you advise Vikas to do next?
qa.a: Write down what was found with dates, talk it through with a trusted adviser outside the office, and use the proper channel, such as the board, instead of waiting for next quarter.

qa.q: What is life like for the girls in the top dorm while this goes on?
qa.a: They put buckets under the leaks every night, bearing the cost of a decision they know nothing about.

grounding: Vikas's letter shows loyalty to a boss and team pulling against conscience, with fear of being called a traitor outweighing duty to those harmed.
